title: CREATE INDEX
description: An index lets Postgres find matching rows without scanning the whole table - the tradeoff is it costs disk space and slows down writes to that column a little. Create an index named `idx_orders_customer_id` on `orders.customer_id`, a column that's frequently filtered on.
hints: 💡 SQL concept to consider: CREATE INDEX

CREATE INDEX <index_name> ON <table> (<column>) - the index name is yours to choose, but it needs to be unique across the whole database, which is why a idx_<table>_<column> naming convention is common.
Name the index idx_orders_customer_id, on the orders table, over the customer_id column.
expected_behavior: Creates a B-tree index on orders.customer_id, speeding up queries that filter or join on it.
explanation: Without an index, Postgres has to scan every row in orders to find matches (a sequential scan) - with one, it can jump straight to the matching rows instead, which matters a lot once a table has real volume.
postgres_note: Postgres indexes default to the B-tree type, good for equality and range queries (=, <, >, BETWEEN) - other types (GIN, GiST, hash) exist for specialized cases like full-text search.
